headline: next-yak concatenates the three-level chain into one `__yak_button` at build time and leads the field, while the css prop keeps a merge at every level and finishes below hand-written vanilla.

microbench.why: Three components, each contributing its own declarations and threading `className` down, so the measurement turns on what survives to render. `next-yak` compiles the chain to `__yak_button("yOURrPB yOURrPB1 yOURrPB2")`, one component carrying all three levels' classes, and leads at 1.45M renders/s. `vanilla` at 1.33M keeps its three functions and joins strings at each one. The css prop cannot collapse a chain: `next-yak-css` calls `mergeCssProp` once per level and falls to 938,000, below `next-yak-nofold` at 1.30M, which is the sharpest evidence in the suite that the two next-yak APIs behave differently under composition. `emotion` at 447,000 re-serializes the merged rules for every instance.

autocannon.why: `next-yak` at 1,225 req/s and `vanilla` at 1,155 lead, with `next-yak-nofold` at 1,097 showing the same chain unfolded. `panda` finishes last at 340 req/s, an order below the leaders, because three object resolutions per instance all happen inside the request.

attribution.why: `vanilla` at 0.803 ms and `next-yak` at 0.806 ms are tied by different routes: one books 0.255 ms of component self-time for three functions, the other 0.365 ms of lib self-time for a single folded wrapper. `next-yak-css` needs 1.24 ms because `mergeCssProp` runs at every level, split across 0.142 ms of lib and 0.488 ms of component self-time. `panda` at 1.93 ms re-resolves each level's style object.

hydrate.why: The css-prop lanes separate sharply on this axis: `next-yak-css` needs 91.7 ms against 47.7 ms for the styled lane on the identical chain, because `mergeCssProp` runs again per level while the client walks the tree. `next-yak-nofold` at 46.4 ms and `bamboo` at 47.1 ms lead, and `emotion` at 111 ms and `goober` at 100 ms rebuild sheets as usual.

inp.why: Thirteen lanes answer one click between 6.8 ms and 8.1 ms, flat given the spread. `goober` at 10.5 ms and `emotion` at 9.5 ms are the only separations worth naming.

mount.why: Twelve lanes mount inside a 71.0 ms to 86.3 ms band, `next-yak-nofold` first at 71.0 ms with `next-yak` at 72.3 ms. Layout dominates the measurement and is identical across lanes, so composition depth barely registers here.

renderTiming.why: One style recalculation per lane, between 0.127 ms and 0.180 ms. Composition changes what runs inside React, not what the style engine has to match afterwards.

payload.why: `vanilla` is the floor at 3,044 gz B with no JS. `next-yak-css` adds 346 B of runtime and `next-yak` 1,152 B. Depth costs the compile-time lanes almost nothing on the wire, since three levels of declarations gzip into roughly the sheet one level produces. The runtime lanes ship 13 kB or more of JS whatever the depth.

nsweep.why: `next-yak` holds 2.57 ms at the largest size against 2.92 ms for its no-fold lane and 3.98 ms for the css prop, so a per-level merge sets a slope that the folded chain never acquires. `panda` at 9.32 ms and `emotion` at 9.30 ms bend hardest.

crossCase: Bracketed by the Examples `compose-1` and `compose-6`. `next-yak` runs the three depths at 2.27M, 1.45M and 1.49M renders/s, so the cost lands entirely on the first wrapper and everything after it is free. `vanilla` pays once per level, 1.96M to 1.33M to 919,000, and `next-yak-css` pays once per level too, 2.05M to 938,000 to 615,000.
